explanations.explanation: This neuron is basically a “word-start” detector for content-rich terms: it lights up on the very first subtoken of a capitalized or special keyword (proper names, titles, acronyms, hyphen-compounds, accented syllables, etc.), marking the start of a salient word in headings, lists or titles.

This neuron flags discourse cues that introduce or weigh factors—especially the “take … into …” pattern (into account/into consideration) and related add-to or in-so constructions—that signal “consider this” transitions in an argument.

This feature fires on tokens that introduce or label structured, ordered entries—e.g. “Description,” “Step 2,” list-item numbers or bullets, date/month/day markers, ordinal positions (3)), betting codes (1X2), etc. In other words, it detects enumeration or section-heading markers in semi-structured text.

This neuron is a subword‐boundary detector – it fires on the little token fragments that mark the start of the second segment of a compound word or CamelCased name (e.g. “flu” in in-flu-encers, “Sh” in Sh-ower, “St” in St-ickers, “ab” in Dat-ab-ricks, “Sc” in Sc-odelario, etc.).

This neuron is not really looking at content words but at little grammatical “add-ons” across scripts—short function-word or affix/diacritic tokens.  It lights up on English modal auxiliaries (may, might, could), Korean case particles (을/를), the Chinese 次 “once,” the Japanese prolonged-sound mark ー, Indic vowel signs like ি/ে, etc.  In other words, it’s a detector for those small, semantically light affix or particle tokens rather than full lexical stems.

This feature fires on the bits of a text that qualify or sharpen meaning—especially hyphens in compound adjectives and nearby tokens, plus adverbs and adjectives that signal degree or emphasis (e.g. “high-quality,” “far bigger,” “more detail,” “scientifically,” “percent,” “new,” “same,” “clean,” etc.). It marks the little words and dashes that intensify, specify or distinguish key concepts.

This feature fires on the conventional “opening move” of a forum Q&A post—i.e. the initial phrasing that kicks off a question or thread (interrogative starters like “How…,” “Does…,” “Why…,” self-introductions (“I figured…,” “I’m…”) dates/times, greetings, etc.). It’s a marker for the speech-act of launching a help or discussion request.
This neuron fires on vague or non-specific quantity words—indefinite quantifiers like “lot,” “handful,” “plenty,” “one,” “hundreds,” etc., that signal an approximate or abundant amount.

This neuron fires on subword pieces that form the second half of compound tokens (hyphen-ated or camel-cased words)—essentially marking continuation segments or “suffix” fragments in multi-part terms.

This feature lights up on tokens that serve as structured numeric labels or separators—e.g. dates (Mar 3, 9/28/19), list/section headings (Level 19, Practice #30, § 173-4), rounds or quarters (Round 5, Q3), verse refs (1:5), sticker numbers (N° 403), license codes (CL 3/898/2013) etc.—in short, the markup around enumeration or identifier numbers.
This feature detects lower‐bound quantitative comparisons—the “more than/over <N>” pattern signaling a minimum threshold in formal, fact‐style statements.

This feature fires on the repeated, emphasized multi‐word proper names that serve as page or section headings—e.g. brand, product or site names presented in title‐style across marketing or catalog text.

This neuron fires on the small prepositions (at / in / on, plus occasional intensifiers like even) when they head a brief locative or stative phrase—i.e. the “at X,” “in Y,” or “on Z” constructions that introduce a condition, state, or setting.

This neuron fires on the “lead” word of a multi-word formal label or title—typically a title-case qualifier at the head of named entities, ranks or official names (e.g. “Critical” in Critical Care, “Top” in Top 10/Top Gear, “New” in New York/New Jersey, “Best” in Best Animated Feature, “Chief” in Chief of Staff, the “nsic” in Forensic, “saturated” in monounsaturated fats, “of” in Bachelor of Arts, etc.).

This neuron fires on the kernel of a bound root—especially Latin‐derived stems—marking the start of contentful morphemes (e.g. lett-, cult-, minister-, associ-, acknowled-, eleg-, intervent-, reun-) across words and languages.
This feature detects the repeated boilerplate metadata block of blog entries (e.g. “This entry was posted on … and is filed under … You can follow any responses … through the RSS feed …”).
This neuron is a negative‐polarity detector: it lights up on negation markers (not/never/contracted “n’t” etc.) that signal denial, failure or exception in a clause.
This feature detects numeric quantity tokens—numbers (often with decimals) that express measurements, dimensions, counts, dosages, dates, percentages, etc., within text.
This feature flags when the text expresses dependence or focused attention—words and idioms like “rely on,” “depend on,” or “keep an eye on.”

This neuron fires on the lexical heads of common linking phrases—especially prepositional or infinitival constructions—that signal cause, purpose, time or relation (e.g. “due to,” “designed to,” “end of,” “years ago,” “leading to”).
